title: Any language (Mishnah Sotah 7:1)
hook: the Shema, Amidah and grace may be said in any language one understands
tomorrow: Siddur close: prayer shapes the day

segments.voice: Yesterday, the zimmun: three at the table, and one invites the rest. Your line was let us bless. Today, which language the blessing has to be in.

Saturday morning, three synagogues, three cities, Hebrew in each of them. But listen closer. In one, the rabbi reads a prayer in English. In another, an old man murmurs a translation in Russian under his breath. In a third, the children sing a line in Spanish. Some people assume Jewish prayer only counts in Hebrew. The Mishnah took up that question long before anyone printed a translated prayer book, and its answer was a list.
screen: `HEBREW IN EACH OF THEM.` → `ENGLISH, RUSSIAN, SPANISH.` → `DOES IT COUNT?`

segments.voice: In tractate Sotah, the Mishnah lists things that may be said in any language. Among them: the Shema, the tefillah, which means the Amidah, and Birkat HaMazon, the grace after meals you met two days ago. The three pillars of daily prayer. The Talmud explains the Shema in a lovely way. Shema means hear, and some sages read it as: hear in any language that you hear, that you understand. If the words don't reach you, what have you heard? Grace is a blessing, and you can't really thank someone in words you don't follow. The Amidah is a plea for mercy, and you plead in whatever words you have. Not everything is on that list. The Mishnah has a second list of things that must be said in Hebrew, like the priestly blessing. And Hebrew holds a special place: the language of the Torah and the prayer book, shared by Jews far apart. Many authorities in Jewish law say it's best to pray in Hebrew if you understand it, and some say Hebrew should be used even if you don't. Reform prayer books include a great deal of the vernacular; Orthodox prayer books keep the Hebrew and print translations beside it. Communities weigh it differently. But the Mishnah's baseline stands: the Shema, the Amidah and grace are valid in a language you understand. In the Mishnah's view, prayer doesn't wait for the right accent.
screen: `THE SHEMA, THE AMIDAH, THE GRACE.` · `SHEMA: HEAR, IN WHAT YOU HEAR.` · `SOME THINGS STAY IN HEBREW.` · `COMMUNITIES WEIGH IT DIFFERENTLY.` · then, large: `ANY LANGUAGE.`

segments.voice: Use the language you dreamed in as a child, the one your grandmother scolded you in, and say something slowly in it: a short prayer or blessing if you pray, or something you're grateful for, out loud, if you don't, and notice whether it lands differently. If English is your only language, say it in the plainest English you can, the way you'd say it to a child.
Any language. The Mishnah's ruling that the Shema, the Amidah and the grace after meals may be said in any language you understand.
Your line: God understands every language. Hebrew keeps its place, and your own words count too. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Many Jewish communities pray mainly in Hebrew, with translations printed beside the text; Reform and some other communities include substantial prayer in the local language, and many individuals add personal prayers in their mother tongue.
